what_it_does: Ray tracing is how video games and film renderers simulate realistic lighting: for each pixel, the computer fires a virtual ray from the camera, figures out what it hits, and traces further rays for reflections and shadows. The geometric scene is organized as a tree of nested bounding boxes (called a BVH — a bounding volume hierarchy) so that the computer can quickly skip geometry the ray cannot possibly hit. The catch is that different rays travel in different directions and hit different parts of the tree, so thousands of rays running in parallel on a graphics chip (a GPU — a chip with thousands of small cores designed to process many things simultaneously) all fetch different tree nodes from memory in an unpredictable order, causing slow memory accesses. Treelet acceleration groups nearby tree nodes into 'treelets' and batches many rays together to traverse the same treelet at once, improving memory reuse. This paper makes that approach practical on GPUs by 'virtualizing' rays — pausing a ray's generating program after it is launched so the GPU core can work on something else, allowing far more rays to be in flight simultaneously and filling the treelets with enough rays to make batching worthwhile.
